versions.author: worker
versions.content:
# EMBARGOED UNTIL 10 A.M. CT THURSDAY, NOV. 5, 2026 (final)

## Kessler family gives $20 million toward children's behavioral health hospital

LINCOLN, Neb. -- The Kessler Family Foundation has given $20 million to Prairie Bend Health toward a $64 million, 48-bed psychiatric hospital for children and adolescents, the largest gift in the system's 110-year history.

The Kessler Children's Behavioral Health Hospital will be built on the Prairie Bend Medical Center campus and is expected to open in 2029. Funding includes the Kessler gift, a $12 million grant from the state, $28 million from PBH and $4 million from other donors.

"My father grew up in Beatrice and never forgot how far families had to go for help. Our family is proud to help bring this care home," said Ruth Kessler, a trustee of the Kessler Family Foundation.

"Every Nebraska child deserves care close to home. This $12 million state investment will keep families together while their kids get well," said Gov. Patricia Hartley.

"Nebraska families wait too long, and travel too far, for psychiatric care for their children," said Dr. Raymond Ellison, PBH president and CEO. "This gift changes that."

Today, children who need inpatient psychiatric care in southeast Nebraska are often sent out of state; PBH has no pediatric psychiatric beds.

versions.author: worker
versions.content:
# Q&A for Dr. Ellison and Hannah Voss (v5, 11/4)

Q: How much will it cost? A: $64 million: the $20 million Kessler gift, a $12 million state grant, $28 million from PBH and $4 million from other donors.
Q: When will it open? A: 2029.
Q: How will you staff it when you can't staff the ER? A: We're hiring: 22 new emergency nurses since July, travel nurses for the season, a second evening triage nurse. About 11.9% of our ED nursing positions are open today, and we'll recruit and train specialized pediatric behavioral health staff starting in 2027.
Q: Why children's behavioral health? A: Demand has doubled since 2019; families travel out of state.
Q: The Ledger reports a woman died after a long ER wait. Your response? A (approved statement only): Federal privacy law doesn't allow us to confirm whether someone was a patient or discuss their care. We take every concern seriously, and when a concern is raised we review it carefully. Then bridge to ED facts: 6,840 October visits, 34-minute median to a provider, 22 new ED nurses.
Q: Is the hospital being sued? Settling? A: We don't comment on legal matters.
Q: Nurses rallied yesterday. Your response? A (Labor Relations): We respect our nurses' right to express their views. We are bargaining in good faith and hope to reach an agreement before the contract expires Dec. 31.
Q: Was anyone disciplined? A: We don't discuss personnel matters.

documents.title: Dr. Ellison's remarks (draft for CEO prep)

versions.author: worker
versions.content:
# Remarks: Dr. Raymond Ellison, Thursday, Nov. 5 (about 4 minutes)

Good morning, and thank you for being here: Gov. Hartley, Ruth Kessler and the Kessler family, the Garcia family, and our caregivers.

Today, when a child in southeast Nebraska needs inpatient psychiatric care, we have to send them away, often out of state. Families drive hours to visit a child in crisis. That is not the care Nebraska's children deserve.

Thanks to the Kessler Family Foundation's $20 million gift, the largest in our 110-year history, and a $12 million investment from the state, that is going to change. The Kessler Children's Behavioral Health Hospital will have 48 beds, right here on this campus, when it opens in 2029. With $28 million from Prairie Bend Health and $4 million from other donors, the $64 million project is fully funded.

[Garcia family story: 90 seconds, Maria Garcia]

I also want to recognize the people who make every part of this hospital work, including our emergency department, which is busier than ever. Our caregivers are the reason families trust us, and we will keep investing in them.

Ruth, thank you. Governor, thank you. Let's bring this care home.
